Now that there is so much interest in various construction projects, both from the government and from private individuals, the ACM is keeping an eye on the situation. Chair Snoep sees no concrete signs that fraud is taking place on such a large scale today. Offers Construction fraud is still seen in smaller cases, Snoep says. For example, this involves companies that are in contact with each other during a tender for a municipal project to build or improve infrastructure. Companies that have no time for a contract must still submit a bid. After discussing the price, the party with no interest then places its bid just above the other bids. In this way, the offer of the party that does want the contract appears more attractive. The ACM will present the first conclusions of its investigation into construction fraud next year.

title: Cell shortage continues, more prisoners released early
lead: <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> wants, as a last resort, to send prisoners home up to four weeks before the end of their sentence. This is necessary because of the cell shortage, writes <entity id="person:claudia-van-bruggen">staatssecretaris Van Bruggen</entity> (Justice) in a letter to Parliament. Last year it was already decided to release some prisoners up to two weeks early. That applied only to prisoners with a prison sentence of up to one year. Now it will also apply to prisoners with a prison sentence of up to two years. Prisoners who committed a sex offence are not eligible for early release. Until now there was enough room for women in prison. But because part of their cells is now used by male detainees, there is now also a cell shortage for women. Therefore the measure will from now on also apply to women, although they are expected to be sent home at most two weeks early. No more space at police stations. Due to various causes there is less space in prisons. For example, the prisons in Veenhuizen and Sittard are currently being renovated, so fewer prisoners can be held there. In addition, dozens of detainees are held in police station cells, although they should actually be in prison. That number is still rising. Van Bruggen says that without new expansions, detainees will have to be sent home. "I acknowledge that this is a bitter message for our society and in particular for victims", she writes in the letter to Parliament. "All efforts are aimed at preventing impunity and winding down the temporary emergency measures as quickly as responsibly possible."

title: Renewed mass strike at clothing factories in Bangladesh
lead: In Bangladesh, dozens of clothing factories have again closed today in protest. Workers in the garment industry are striking for higher wages. The actions are part of a larger wave of protest that has been going on for some time. Last weekend, already 150 clothing factories in the country closed their doors, and a motorway between the capital Dhaka and the northern city of Tangail near Gazipur was blocked. Factory workers also downed tools at the end of October. The workers demand a higher minimum wage of 30,000 taka per month, equivalent to 220 euros. The current minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is less than half that, 90 euros per month. Workers say this is not enough to cope with the rising cost of living. Years without inflation adjustment Inflation in Bangladesh is high: in October prices were 8 percent higher than a year earlier. In recent years the gap between prices and wages in Bangladesh has grown steadily. Factory workers have not had an inflation adjustment for three years. The country is also being hard hit by the unrest in the Middle East and around the Strait of Hormuz. Bangladesh is heavily dependent on imports of fuels such as oil and LNG, much of which is transported via that sea route. The clothing industry is of crucial importance to Bangladesh. After China, the country is the world's largest clothing exporter. The sector accounts for about 80 percent of the country's export income, generates around 38 billion dollars a year and provides work for more than 4 million people. Talks at a standstill From H&M, Zara, C&A to Primark: many major international, but also Dutch brands have their clothing made in Bangladesh. Factory owners and politicians fear that clothing chains will move to other production countries if the unrest continues. Two weeks ago an agreement seemed to be in the making between the wage commission and the trade unions, but that is now at a standstill. Planned negotiations were cancelled today for unclear reasons. It is therefore uncertain whether the workers will actually receive higher pay. Many workers wonder whether their demands are being taken seriously. At the same time, striking is not without risk. Workers who lay down their tools lose pay. Moreover, some protests have a political dimension. Among the demonstrators are supporters of the ousted <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. For them the actions are not only about wages and working conditions, but also about discontent with the current government. Summer collection What the current unrest means for clothing exports to Europe is still unclear. Earlier, chains said production for the upcoming summer collections was not in danger despite factories shutting down. But traditionally a lot of clothing is exported from Bangladesh at the end of the year. Employers therefore have an interest in quickly sitting down at the table with the striking factory workers. In addition, in the first nine months of this year, clothing exports from Bangladesh to the European Union fell by 12 percent. This has several causes, including growing competition from other production countries, such as China and Vietnam.

title: Small and medium-sized businesses do not have the basics of cybersecurity in order
lead: Small and medium-sized businesses (mkb'ers) face a substantial risk of becoming victims of a cyberattack. The National Coordinator for Counterterrorism and Security (NCTV) warns of this. According to the security service, simple basic cybersecurity measures are often missing. These are measures that businesses can sometimes easily take. For example, 5 percent of the mkb does not use antivirus software, according to the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek</entity> (CBS). Businesses sometimes also use weak passwords: 17 percent of the mkb has no arrangements to prevent that. An extra security layer at login is also often missing. For example, that an employee must enter an extra access code alongside a password. In the cybersecurity world this is called MFA: multi-factor authentication. This protection makes a hack much harder. Yet 18 percent of mkb'ers do not apply the measure. "Most hacks are not the exciting cyberattacks you see in films", says Martine Groen. She conducts research into cybersecurity at the mkb at the Utrecht University of Applied Sciences. "Usually it happens because of silly mistakes, such as an easy-to-guess password." Insufficient attention to security: 'Dangerous cocktail' People at Royal Dirkzwager know how things can go wrong. This company monitors shipping for ports, among others. In March 2023 the company was digitally held hostage: everything on the computer servers was locked. A criminal group demanded a ransom to make the files accessible again. "That was a dangerous situation", says Nicolas Maes, head of IT at the company. "For example, we also monitor shipping traffic around drilling platforms, so that no ships sail where they should not be. Because of the attack we lost sight of forty drilling platforms. We had to send helicopters out to guard them." The attack could probably have been prevented if Royal Dirkzwager had taken a number of basic security measures, Maes thinks. "Just before that we had moved all our files, computer programmes and IT environment to external computer servers", he says. This means employees can always access company information via the internet. That environment was not well secured. "There was no limit on the number of login attempts someone could make", says Maes. As a result, a hacker could keep trying passwords until one with the right password succeeded. The company also did not have MFA protection, Maes says. "I'm a bit ashamed to say that, because it was a dangerous cocktail. During that move we paid insufficient attention to IT security. These are a few small measures that we now say: if only we had taken them then." 'Big and structural problem' The absence of those basic measures is a structural problem, the NCTV warns. For example, the security service also sees that businesses do not actively monitor their business network, so that they could catch intruders. "You want an alarm to go off when an attacker gets in", says Vaisha Bernard of security company Eye Security. "That is why you need a kind of camera system on your network." Yet 37 percent of mkb'ers do not do that. A roughly equally large group does not keep records of how computer networks or systems are used. As a result, after a cyberattack no investigation can take place into what a hacker had access to. "A lot of attention in the media goes to big attacks on well-known companies", says Harm Teunis of security company ESET. "What you don't hear about is all those mkb'ers that fall victim to a cyberattack every year and have employee or customer data stolen." "Small businesses often spend less money on cybersecurity. Entrepreneurs are afraid it will take a big bite out of their turnover. Strict requirements also apply to large companies. For many mkb'ers that is not the case." 'Mkb often postpones cybersecurity' Large companies often have specialists or entire departments dealing with cybersecurity, says researcher Groen of the Utrecht University of Applied Sciences. "That is not possible in the mkb. That expertise is often missing. Entrepreneurs do think cybersecurity is really important. But they are always busy, so it is often postponed." That is why she believes mkb'ers should get more support, for example from trade associations. If those figure out a lot for businesses in their sector, entrepreneurs do not have to do it themselves. This way mkb'ers can get very concrete advice to improve their cybersecurity." The cyberattack on Royal Dirkzwager was a valuable lesson for the company, Maes says. "We have taken those basic measures since then", he says. "My advice to other businesses: arrange this now. And not when it is too late."

title: Arrests after multiple finds of illegal fireworks in the Rotterdam region
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> found large quantities of illegal fireworks at several locations in Rotterdam and surroundings last week. These include cobra's, nitrates and lawinepijlen. Several people have been arrested, the youngest suspect of whom is 16 years old, the police announced today. The biggest find was last week on Wednesday in a house in Maassluis. There the police found ten boxes with 1,500 pieces of illegal fireworks. The exact type is not known, but according to the police the fireworks are "equivalent to cobra's". A 25-year-old man from Maassluis has been arrested. It also happened in Rotterdam that day. In a house in the IJsselmonde district there were 200 pieces of illegal fireworks. The police held a 21-year-old Rotterdammer responsible. He, like the man from Maassluis, is still in custody. Mortar bombs In Zwijndrecht officers found 116 so-called shells (mortar bombs). Shells, like cobra's, are illegal. The fireworks have been seized and a 20-year-old man from Zwijndrecht has been detained, the regional broadcaster Rijnmond reports. Shells were also found in Puttershoek. That happened on Saturday 8 November in a garage box. The stuff was hidden, among other places, in a canvas bag. "All extremely dangerous to store like that in a garage box", the police say about it. Nobody has been arrested for this find yet, but the investigation is ongoing. Teenagers arrested In a house in Nieuw-Beijerland the police found multiple nitrates and banger fireworks that same weekend. A 16-year-old boy has been arrested. The police searched his house after he was caught setting off heavy fireworks at a skate park. The teenager is not in custody but will have to answer to the judge later, the police say. A 17-year-old boy from Oud-Beijerland has also been arrested. That happened earlier this month already, on Monday 2 November, after a firework find in a sea container on an industrial estate. In it the police found 63 cobra's, shells and lawinepijlen.

title: Six months in prison for 26-year-old man who shot cats with a crossbow
lead: 26-year-old Yihui L. has been sentenced to 181 days in prison for killing and injuring cats with a crossbow in Eindhoven. One cat did not survive this. Between November 2025 and May of this year, the 26-year-old L. hit five cats with an arrow in a residential area. In May, a cat was fatally injured. The owner found the pet with the arrow in its eye in front of their house. The injured cats were hit, among other places, in their paw or just beside their eye. They were also found by their owners with an arrow in their little bodies. The judge holds L. seriously to account for not having considered the impact on the owners of the animals. The case caused great unrest in the neighbourhood. Residents did not know whether their cat could still safely go outside. In addition, the man shot the cats with a crossbow in a residential area, according to the judge. L. stated that he was aware this was dangerous and that he therefore chose to shoot in the evening. 'Deliberately hunting' The man has admitted that he shot at the cats. L. "really went hunting for cats in the area", the public prosecutor said when demanding the sentence. He stated that he was, among other things, angry because a cat had scratched him when he tried to catch it with cat food. His rage was intensified after he stepped in cat faeces in the forest. During the interrogations he expressed regret for his actions. Diminished criminal responsibility The sentence is lower than the nine-month prison term demanded by the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity>. In setting the sentence, the court took into account that L. has shown remorse and has proactively reached a compensation arrangement with the majority of the cats' owners. It also counts that the man has diminished criminal responsibility. A disorder within the autism spectrum has been established in the suspect. The risk of reoffending is low according to the psychologist, the court said.

title: Boat with migrants went into the water near the village of Hoofdplaat, two suspects remain in custody for longer
lead: The rubber boat with 38 people on board, which the coastguard intercepted in <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity> at the end of last month, went into the water near the village of Hoofdplaat in the <entity id="org:gemeente-sluis">gemeente Sluis</entity>. That is what the Public Prosecution Service (OM) reports in a statement. Investigations have shown that the people on board had gone from France to the Zeeland village of Breskens. In the night of Friday 30 to Saturday 31 October 2026 they then set out onto the Westerschelde near Hoofdplaat. The rubber boat was however quickly spotted on radar images from the Coastguard. The rescue services intervened at the height of Cadzand. Because the vessel's engine was missing, the boat had become adrift. The migrants were taken to the marina in Cadzand. The engine is still being searched for. Pre-trial detention extended There were 38 people on board in total: 36 migrants and two smugglers. Six of those on board were minors. The pre-trial detention of the two Sudanese men, who are suspected of aiding human smuggling, has been extended by thirty days. One of the two suspects is 21 years old, and the other says he is a minor, according to the OM. They are no longer under restrictions. On the way to the United Kingdom According to the OM, it has been established after investigation that all those on board were heading for the United Kingdom. A large number of those on board have been heard as witnesses, the OM writes. A number of phones have been analysed.

title: Tax on wealth splits cabinet: this is what else changed in the tax plan
lead: Last week, politics was largely about a tax increase for the wealthy. That measure was added to the tax plan, which sets out the government's revenue for next year, on the initiative of PRO and Volt. But the increase in tax on wealth is not the only thing that has been changed by various parties in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. Here is what else is in the plan, partly based on inventories by tax advisory firms EY and KPMG Meijburg. Box 3 First, a bit more on the tax increase on wealth. From 2029 there will be two rates for Box 3 tax. Instead of one rate of 36 percent on all capital gains above a threshold of 1,800 euros a year, you will pay 35.5 percent on the first 60,000 euros, and 38.5 percent on everything above that. So if you only have savings, you will in fact pay less tax if you receive less than 61,800 euros in savings interest in a year. If you sell shares or property, for example, with a substantial profit, you may reach that top rate sooner. Because if such assets increase in value by more than 61,800 euros in the years from 2029, you will pay 38.5 percent tax on the amount above that. This does not apply to the sale of your own home, incidentally. Income tax The tax rate of the first bracket of income tax will be 35.84 percent instead of the planned 36.23 percent in 2027. On the first roughly 39,000 euros of gross salary, you will therefore pay slightly less tax than previously planned. Private jet flight tax In 2030, a high flight tax for private jets will be introduced. That was already the plan, but the tax will now be higher than previously planned. For each distance category it will be 100 euros higher. That makes it 520 euros per passenger for short flights, 1,115 euros for medium distances and 2,200 euros for long-haul flights. The tax applies to flights with fewer than twenty passenger seats. Inheritance and gift tax not indexed The tax brackets for inheritance and gift tax will not be indexed for five years, from 2027 up to and including 2031. Normally those amounts rise each year to keep pace with inflation. But now they will remain the same for five years. So you will start paying inheritance and gift tax sooner than the plan envisaged. For gift tax on children, for example, the limits are now 6,908 euros and 158,669 euros. If a child receives less than 6,908 euros in gifts in a year, they pay no gift tax. On the amount above that exemption and up to 158,669 euros, you pay 10 percent, and 20 percent above that. Paper gifts restricted Giving on paper is being made less attractive. People with a lot of wealth can currently give money on paper, often to children or grandchildren. Then they do not actually give it, but only administratively at the notary. As a result, surviving relatives have to pay less inheritance tax on death. Because less inheritance then remains, you are therefore less likely to fall into the top rate of 20 percent inheritance tax for children or 36 percent for grandchildren. But you can also achieve that by giving in real terms every year rather than only on paper. The major advantage of a paper gift is that the giver must pay as much as 6 percent interest per year on the amount gifted to the recipient. That amount must actually be paid by them. And that is therefore a transfer of wealth without any gift tax having to be paid on it. That high interest rate will be halved to 3 percent from 2028. As a result, giving on paper becomes much less attractive. <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity>? It is also good to know: the parties that voted for the tax plan in the Tweede Kamer narrowly lack a majority in the Eerste Kamer. They account for 35 votes, and a majority requires 38. There are a number of single-member groups in the Eerste Kamer that may vote in favour. And the question is also whether the VVD group will still vote against now that the plan has been passed by the Tweede Kamer. The expectation is that the Eerste Kamer will vote on the tax plan in mid-December.

title: Fake officers leave deep scars: 'I did not manage to watch over the belongings of my late wife'
lead: The number of incidents involving fake officers has risen to a record high this year, it emerged today. Fraudsters posing as <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and bank employees specifically target older people, whom they relieve of money and jewellery. Victims afterwards cannot understand how they fell for it. As a warning, three of them tell their story. Jo Bosma (93): 'People, please be careful' "Around eight o'clock in the evening I was called by a bank employee. He said: 'All sorts of things are going on, and they have also withdrawn amounts from your account.'" Fortunately the criminals had been caught, said the so-called bank employee. One of them was even said to have had Mr Bosma's address on him. To determine the value of the items the thieves had wanted to steal, the fake bank employee sent a 'detective'. This fake officer was not wearing a police uniform. He did have a hood up. According to himself, that was because he must not be recognised as a detective. Guilt Bosma handed him his bank card and the jewellery of his late wife, with whom he had been for seventy years. Only once the fake detective had left did Bosma realise that he had been robbed. "I was brainwashed. You are manipulated so much that you don't notice it." The next morning he was called again by the 'bank employee', presumably to prise his PIN code out of him. "I said: 'You are a fraudster!' Then he hung up." The theft, at the beginning of this month, has caused him sleepless nights. The guilt is great. "I was supposed to watch over my wife's belongings and I didn't manage it. That has given a huge dent to my self-esteem. It is actually the worst thing that has ever happened to me. I want to shout it from the rooftops: people, please be careful." Greet Kuitert (81): 'Have a glass of water, we will help you' She had actually warned friends about the dangers of fraudsters. And yet this year she fell for it herself too, Greet Kuitert tells RTV Noord. "I remember that my friend had been caught in WhatsApp fraud. She had received a message, supposedly from her son, asking for money to pay for his laptop. It cost 2,200 euros. I said how stupid she had been. But a little later I was called myself and I too was caught up in it." Like many others, Kuitert was approached by a so-called employee of her bank. Supposedly 1,500 euros would be taken from her account. She became quite panicked. "Madam, calm down, there's nothing wrong, I was told. 'Have a glass of water, we will help you', the man said." Stubborn For hours she sat on the phone with the fraudster to solve the problem that had been invented. Eventually someone came round to collect her debit card. Madam Kuitert also entrusted this fake officer with her PIN code. "I don't understand how I could have been so silly. And all the while I still had that man on the phone. I kept saying: 'A bank doesn't do this, a bank doesn't do this.' But that man kept insisting: 'Madam Kuitert, don't be so stubborn.'" Psychologists When the bank employee advised her to hand over her jewellery as well, she refused. After the fake officer had left, she had her bank card blocked as quickly as possible. By then it turned out that 700 euros had already been withdrawn from her account. She should not blame herself, the police told her. "That officer said: 'They are like psychologists. They spend sixty hours a week doing nothing but this'." Margo de Bruine: 'She is angry at the whole world' Her mother has never been the same again after she was robbed by a fake officer, Margo de Bruine tells Omroep Zeeland. "She has been left with post-traumatic stress disorder. She is angry at the whole world." Two years ago her 87-year-old mother fell victim to fraudsters. Here too the story was that people with bad intentions were wandering around the neighbourhood and that the police would send someone to secure valuables. Wedding ring Before long a fake officer was also standing at De Bruine's mother's door, for whom she had to pick out her jewellery. When she had laid everything out, he demanded that she take off her wedding ring. The fake officer also had her hand over her watch, a necklace, a gold bracelet and her bank cards. He withdrew 800 euros with those cards. The man has been tracked down and convicted. He showed little remorse, De Bruine says. "Because he thought himself very pitiful. He had to look after his father. He had to look after his little brother. He had to look after his little sister. All sorts of things were dragged up. That certainly sticks with me."

title: King commemorates American salute, Sint Eustatius honours its own freedom fighters
lead: On Sint Eustatius, <entity id="person:willem-alexander">koning Willem-Alexander</entity> commemorated the historic salute to the United States 250 years ago. But for many islanders, 16 November is above all Statia Day: a celebration of their own culture and history. On the island there is growing attention for people who resisted slavery. Close to Fort Oranje, where in 1776 the American flag was greeted with cannon fire, a mural of Thomas Dupersoy and other leaders of the 1848 slave revolt was unveiled this weekend. Their portraits now hang in Oranjestad, close to the spot where the king commemorated the American salute. First recognition On 16 November 1776 the American warship Andrew Doria entered the harbour. It fired a salute, which was returned from Fort Oranje on the orders of the Dutch governor Johannes de Graaff. This is regarded as the first foreign recognition of the American flag, a few months after the declaration of independence. Sint Eustatius was at that time an important trading port. Through the island, weapons, gunpowder and supplies reached the American rebels. Today that history was commemorated with speeches, flags and the re-enactment of the salute shots. The American ambassador Joe Popolo was also present. Prime Minister <entity id="person:rob-jetten">Rob Jetten</entity> cancelled his visit because of the political crisis in The Hague. Freedom for whom? The celebration is sensitive for a large number of Statians. While the Americans were fighting for their freedom, thousands of people on Sint Eustatius lived in slavery. The governor who had the salute returned was himself a slaveholder. The island was also a hub in the trade in enslaved Africans. The St. Eustatius Afrikan Burial Ground Alliance, led by Kenneth Cuvalay, describes the jubilee primarily as a Dutch-American affair. The organisation asked for the international commemoration to be held in The Hague. It also believes that residents have not had a say. The Dutch <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> disputes this. According to The Hague, Sint Eustatius itself decides how Statia Day is celebrated and the king is a guest there. Willem-Alexander reflects on slavery Willem-Alexander also spoke at Fort Oranje about the history of slavery. He recalled the thousands of Africans who arrived on the island in dehumanising conditions. "No salute on arrival for them", he said. The king referred to research he had commissioned himself into the role of his ancestors. It shows that Dutch stadtholders and kings actively supported colonialism and slavery for centuries. He said he felt connected to the Statians who still experience the consequences. The revolt of 12 June 1848 is receiving a great deal of attention on Sint Eustatius these days. Thomas Dupersoy and five enslaved men then rose up against colonial rule. They demanded freedom, better food rations and shorter working days. The revolt was crushed by force. Their history is also told in the illustrated children's book Courage on Golden Rock, which was presented last weekend. The authors describe the freedom fighters as people with their own talents and desires. Joseph learns to read, Prince knows how the sugar mill works and Abraham gives others courage with song and stories. Mother Betsy brings women together to support the resistance. The book combines historical events with narrative scenes. Last Friday, moreover, the remains of 69 ancestors from the period of slavery were reburied. Their graves had been opened in 2021 during archaeological research. That led to protests. The Statians involved wanted their ancestors to be given a dignified resting place again and for them to be involved from now on in decisions about their heritage. Their own public holiday For the Statians, 16 November has long been more than just the day of the American salute. Statia Day has become their own public holiday, on which they celebrate their culture, music, history and above all their people. There have been festivities throughout the whole weekend. On large murals in Oranjestad, older islanders who have meant a great deal to the community are also honoured. The king cycled past these portraits today. Interest in their own resistance heroes is not unique to Sint Eustatius. On the other Caribbean islands and in Suriname too, the history of slavery is being re-examined and retold. In doing so, people who resisted their oppression are receiving more attention. Much of what we know about these people comes from the archives of colonial officials, plantation owners and courts. In those, rebels were often described as criminals and troublemakers. Historians are now also reading those documents from the perspective of the people who were oppressed. In doing so they use oral traditions, church and plantation registers and archaeological finds. People who were prosecuted by colonial authorities at the time are now placed in the perspective of the resistance and honoured as freedom fighters. On Sint Eustatius this is done with murals, books and commemorations. The six men of the 1848 revolt are thereby given a place alongside the historical figures who have been commemorated for centuries. The king also paid attention to the history of slavery and the involvement of his own ancestors. But the Alliance's criticism is not only about the content of the commemoration. Cuvalay wants Statians themselves to be able to decide which stories are told and who is honoured on their national holiday.

title: Elections are no option in municipal coalition crises: 'Have a drink together'
lead: A patch-up attempt, a new formation or new elections after all? Those are the options D66, VVD and CDA have had since they landed in a coalition crisis last week. The <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">Tweede Kamer</entity> in any case does not want a cabinet collapse, should it come to that, to lead directly to new elections. In provincial and local politics they already have experience in patching up coalition breaches. 'You have to hold a mirror up to the parties.' Municipalities and provinces do not hold early elections. The date for Provincial States and municipal council elections is fixed, always four years after the previous elections. When a coalition crisis arises in local or provincial politics before then, there are no interim elections and they have to find a way out. Three more years until elections This is what happened in 2019 in <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity>, for example. After a political crisis, a split arose in the coalition of VVD, D66, GroenLinks and PvdA. 'We wanted to reopen the financial agreements to avoid having to cut spending on care. The parties could not agree on that,' says Cathelijne Bouwkamp, then alderman on behalf of GroenLinks. GroenLinks and PvdA then pulled the plug on the governing agreement. With almost three years still to go until the next elections, a solution had to be found for the city administration. The then Gelderland VVD deputy Jan Markink and the Amsterdam GroenLinks alderman Rutger Groot Wassink were asked to help look for one. They were given the role of scouts, as is always done after elections. 'Can it still be patched up?' The two men got to work and mainly did a lot of talking. 'With all factions, both coalition and opposition,' says Markink. 'Then you get a picture and make the judgement: can it still be patched up, or is it a coalition breach?' 'Those conversations made clear that the other parties did not fancy forming a new coalition,' recalls Bouwkamp, then alderman. Adding other parties to the coalition was also not the preferred option numerically, according to Groot Wassink. 'Not everyone was happy about it, but we concluded that the four parties had to carry on together,' recalls Groot Wassink. That was not easy, because besides the concrete point of contention over care costs, the two scouts saw a much bigger problem: the poisoned mutual relationships. 'Channelling distrust' So what do you do? 'Talk a lot,' says Groot Wassink. 'We have in fact held a mirror up to everyone,' says Markink. 'We got faction leaders and faction members together and said: pay attention to what you are doing.' Putting agreements on paper also helps, Groot Wassink explains. 'You basically just make working agreements: how are you going to deal with each other?' An example of such an agreement is that coalition partners will not surprise each other with motions and will consult each other if one of the partners has objections. 'Rules of that kind are a way to channel existing distrust,' the former GroenLinks scout summarises. But more important, in his view, is for example to go out for a bite to eat together and so work on the mutual relationships. 'Have a drink together and put the grievances on the table, because if you don't voice them, they keep festering beneath the surface,' Groot Wassink explains. Cathelijne Bouwkamp, then GroenLinks alderman, recognises this too. 'You really have to be able to put everything on the table that is important to you and where it hurts you in the way the other acts. That is quite difficult in a sometimes hostile atmosphere, but it is really important.' In the end, after many conversations, they managed to improve the mutual relations and let the four Arnhem coalition parties continue together. 'Politics is a struggle of ideals, but you cannot keep trying to outdo each other all the time,' says Bouwkamp. 'If politics is only about winning, we will all lose. There is a time for campaigning and a time for governing,' Bouwkamp wants to pass on. 'Then you have to soften, listen to each other and grant each other something.'

title: Turkish farmer in the Antalya region, where the climate summit is being held, struggles with sustainability
lead: Turkey welcomed world leaders last week who gathered for the climate summit in Antalya. Notable was the absence of several leaders, including <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, President Macron and Chancellor Merz. This did not stop Turkish President Erdoğan from stressing shared responsibility in his speech. "We have only one roof over our house: the sky, and we have only one garden: the earth." Green ambitions Turkey For host country Turkey, the summit is an important moment to show its own green ambitions. It wants to position itself clearly as a country that is serious about the energy transition. Turkey aims to be climate neutral by 2053. It is investing in renewable energy, such as large wind and solar parks. Even so, it remains heavily dependent on coal. Agriculture also faces challenges. The Antalya region is known as a holiday destination, but the area also has rich and fertile farmland. In many villages, farming life is passed down from generation to generation. Grandparents and great-grandparents once began growing fruit there. So did the family of agricultural entrepreneur Tevfik Tekin. Drought and floods, 30 per cent of harvest lost In his mandarin orchards he sees the effects of climate change. Where drought was mainly the problem last year, this year they had to deal with floods, Tekin says. "Last year our problem was that it did not rain at all. This year we are dealing with too much water." He had to throw away as much as 30 per cent of his harvest. Too much water in particular can have serious consequences. When roots stand under water for long periods, they can rot and bacterial diseases can develop. "You can compare it with raising a child. The more stress a child experiences while growing up, the greater the chance it will develop psychological problems later in life." Tekin has two jobs, because making a living from growing fruit alone is not possible, he says. In his view, today's agriculture must adapt to the changing climate. "We must also be able to drain the excess water we get from our farmland." High production costs, inflation The government supports farmers with billions of Turkish lira. Farmers receive subsidies, cheap loans and help with damage to their harvest. "But that is still not enough to solve the problems," says Tekin. Because there are also economic problems. Due to inflation, farmers are struggling with high production costs. Diesel and fertiliser, for example, are very expensive because of taxes. According to Tekin, it is so complicated that farmers have to concern themselves with much more than just their crops. "Nowadays we have to constantly make forecasts about future dollar exchange rates and wonder how the prices of fertiliser and other inputs will develop. We are really a bit of an economist too." That financial pressure makes it difficult to invest in sustainability. There are Turkish farmers who work with artificial intelligence. The ambition is there to make agriculture more future-proof. Tevfik also believes in the possibilities of innovation and sustainability, but stresses that farmers cannot achieve this alone. Even so, he tries to remain optimistic. His love of farming life and nature motivates him to keep going. "Once you get used to this life, you cannot let go of it. I do it because I love it."

title: Dirt-cheap groceries thanks to 'budget brand war', but prices will rise again
lead: A pack of stroopwafels for 28 cents, a jar of red cabbage for 26 cents and a pack of wild rice for 45 cents? Some groceries have become dirt cheap in recent months. How can that be, while energy prices and inflation are rising? Some products have fallen in price this year: the cheapest pack of stroopwafels cost 78 cents at the start of this year. And many other products from budget brands, such as jam and peanut butter, now cost only a few tens of cents. "These are absurdly low prices," admits retail professor Laurens Sloot of the University of Groningen. "Supermarkets earn almost nothing on the dirt-cheap products. Sometimes they even add money. But that does not have to be a disaster for them as long as consumers also buy products that still carry a good margin." 'Budget brand war' Sloot says that supermarkets are mainly concerned with the value of "the entire shopping basket" of customers. "Whether there is a price war, I don't know, but perhaps we can now speak of a budget brand war." The main cause of the low prices is consumers' high price sensitivity, says Sloot. That means consumers quickly switch to a cheaper alternative when prices differ between supermarkets. "And if customers switch, supermarkets have to join in this price frenzy." With as large and cheap an assortment of budget products as possible, supermarkets are therefore trying to bind customers. In doing so they closely monitor the prices of competitors' cheapest own brands. When one chain lowers its price by a few cents, the competitor often quickly follows. "It is not as if one supermarket declares a price war, it has gradually emerged," Sloot explains. "Supermarkets want to come out well with organisations such as Kassa and the Consumentenbond, and therefore look at the cheapest items in a product group." "Usually a discounter then comes out as the cheapest. They then use that in their marketing campaigns. Chains such as Plus, Albert Heijn and Jumbo find that annoying and so have to join in this price frenzy." Long-term effect But competition between them is not the only explanation for the low prices. The development of raw material prices on the international market also plays an important role. Many raw materials peaked in price in 2022, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and in 2023, and then fell. Those price falls are not immediately visible in the supermarket. That is because supermarkets and suppliers often make agreements on purchase prices for a year, so it feeds through with a delay into the price consumers pay in the supermarket. Take milk, for example, says Sloot. "A few years ago farmers still got 60 cents per litre for it, which then fell to around 40 cents. That does something to the prices of a pack of milk and a packet of butter." 'Groceries 4 to 7 percent more expensive' With the end of the year in sight, Sloot also thinks the price falls will come to an end. Supermarkets and suppliers are negotiating purchase prices again these months, this time for 2027. Many manufacturers, after a relatively cheaper 2025, are facing rising costs for their raw materials again in 2026. "That will lead to a higher cost price," says Sloot. Energy has become much more expensive because of the Iran war, and supermarkets are paying more in wage costs from 1 January because the youth wage is rising. Professor Sloot therefore expects groceries to become 4 to 7 percent more expensive next year. Negative food inflation Foodstuffs were on average cheaper in August, September and October than a year earlier, <entity id="org:zbo-de-nederlandsche-bank">De Nederlandsche Bank</entity> (DNB) noted last week. So-called negative food inflation is quite exceptional: DNB says it has occurred only in 2021 since 2016. Because food inflation is falling, total inflation is also being curbed, says DNB. That is a sharp contrast with a few years ago, when the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 pushed up prices enormously and food inflation reached as much as 15 percent.

title: Coalition continues with three parties despite accusations, Buma called in to help
lead: Four long days of talks have led to "restoration of trust" between D66, VVD and CDA. The three parties will continue together in the minority cabinet, and for the time being no fourth party is joining. This morning there is an extra <entity id="org:ministerraad">ministerraad</entity>, at which <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> and the deputy prime ministers Yesilgöz and Van den Brink will present their proposal on the continuation of the course of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> to the other ministers. It is already clear that the vice-president of the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity>, <entity id="person:sybrand-van-haersma-buma">Sybrand Buma</entity>, has been asked to help draw up working agreements with opposition parties on the budgets. He will mainly act as an adviser and will not conclude deals himself, according to sources in The Hague. He has a month to do this. Help from RvS chair Buma Buma is vice-chair of the Council of State, an important advisory body to the cabinet. Buma knows <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> well and, after the 2025 House of Representatives elections, when he was <entity id="pos:burgemeester-leeuwarden">burgemeester van Leeuwarden</entity>, he was also informateur. After Friday at the <entity id="org:ministerie-van-algemene-zaken">ministerie van Algemene Zaken</entity>, and on Saturday and Sunday at the De Zwaluwenberg estate in <entity id="org:gemeente-hilversum">Hilversum</entity>, the crisis talks continued on Monday at the Catshuis. The key players left the prime minister's official residence after talking for over eleven hours without speaking to the press. They left it at a statement from the <entity id="org:rijksvoorlichtingsdienst">Rijksvoorlichtingsdienst</entity> (RVD), saying the parties had found each other again "after intensive talks". Details of the agreements have not been made public. Today, Jetten, Yesilgöz and Van den Brink will give an explanation after the ministerraad. Taken by surprise The cabinet and the coalition ran into serious trouble last week, after D66 and CDA reached an agreement with Pro and Volt on a change to the tax plan, under which wealthy people will pay somewhat more tax. The VVD said it felt ambushed by this and called it a bad plan that they could not agree to. The proposal nevertheless received preference in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, after which the VVD decided to vote against the entire tax plan. In the end, D66 and CDA nevertheless managed to secure a majority in the vote, by concluding an agreement with the opposition parties Denk, 50Plus, the ChristenUnie and Partij voor de Dieren. After Friday's talks, VVD leader Yesilgöz called the minority cabinet "a failed experiment that cannot continue like this". She demanded a "political correction" to the course, which she considered too left-leaning. She suggested the possibility of adding an extra, right-wing coalition partner, possibly JA21. In the end, that option was not chosen.

title: Smoking and vaping among mbo students remain popular, alcohol use does decline
lead: Nicotine use among mbo students remains stubbornly high, according to research by the Trimbos Institute. One in five mbo students uses a product containing nicotine every day. The use of alcohol, cannabis and nitrous oxide has decreased compared with 2023. The report is based on figures for 2025. The research focused specifically on mbo students. "Since earlier research shows that the use of alcohol, tobacco and other substances can differ quite a lot between education levels, it is all the more important to continue monitoring the use of mbo students over time," the institute wrote about this earlier. Of the nicotine products, cigarettes remain the most popular among mbo students: nearly one in three students said that in the month before they were surveyed they had smoked; about half of them said they did so daily. The figures have remained almost the same compared with the research of two years earlier. Small decline among vapers Vaping shows a small decline, but here too the figures remain high: one in five mbo students says they have used a vape, of whom 6.4 percent daily. That new nicotine products are not a replacement for cigarettes is also shown by the institute's figures. Of the students who vape daily, more than half (53.8 percent) also smoke cigarettes. A small increase is seen in the use of nicotine pouches, also known as snus. In 2023, 11.6 percent of mbo young people said they had ever used them. In the research carried out in 2025 this rose to 14.3 percent. However, the percentage who use the pouches daily is still low compared with cigarettes and vapes: 1.8 percent. More than non-mbo students Compared with their peers at secondary schools, 16- and 17-year-old mbo students smoke and vape much more: especially the number of daily smokers and vapers is two times (among 16-year-olds) to more than five times (among 17-year-olds) as high, and vaping is also markedly higher. According to the researchers, this is partly because mbo students underestimate the health risk more than their peers do. Set against the stubbornly high nicotine use among mbo young people is that they have drunk less. Since 2021 a decline is visible among young people. There is also one in cannabis use and nitrous oxide. The researchers give no reason for the decline in drug use. For nitrous oxide use an explanation is given: it is less available, partly because of the national ban that took effect in 2023. Mental health For the first time this year, well-being has also been included in the research. More than one in five mbo students struggles with emotional problems. 16- and 17-year-old mbo students on average give a higher score for their well-being than peers who do not go to mbo. "This may be a consequence of the fact that some of these 16- and 17-year-old pupils are in their exam year, so the pressure they experience is (temporarily) higher," the researchers write. "On the other hand, mbo students may be better placed on the course they are following."

title: List of high-risk PFAS contamination sites riddled with errors: 'Government approach is not sound'
lead: A first priority list of PFAS locations to be remediated, compiled by the ministry and more than 40 local authorities, is incorrect. This emerges from an analysis by the NOS and regional broadcasters. Nearly half of the locations are wrongly listed, because it is not yet clear whether they actually pose a risk to the surroundings. According to experts the NOS spoke to, the list is a clear example of a chaotic and slow PFAS approach by the ministry. The result could be that high-risk locations are missed and that other locations are remediated at great expense unnecessarily. In a first annual interim report in May, the ministry reported 57 locations without naming them. According to the ministry, the locations are so polluted that they pose an 'unacceptable risk' to the environment. Last month the list was finally made public under the Open Government Act (Woo). Differing statements An analysis by the NOS and regional broadcasters shows that the list contains many errors. For six of the 57 sites the entry is 'no unacceptable risk', for twenty it is 'not yet known', and for five nothing has been entered on that point. Under the ministry's own definition, nearly half of the locations should therefore be removed. The ministry refers questions about a response to the more than 40 local authorities. Enquiries there have produced no unambiguous explanation. For example, according to the <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">provincie Zuid-Holland</entity>, "the definition was not yet known". The <entity id="org:provincie-noord-holland">provincie Noord-Holland</entity> speaks of its own "administrative error". And according to <entity id="org:gemeente-nijmegen">Nijmegen</entity>, the ministry itself initially asked for 'possibly high-risk locations'. The <entity id="org:provincie-groningen">provincie Groningen</entity> has no locations on the list at all; its submissions were delivered "not in the format" of the ministry. PFAS PFAS is a group of thousands of chemical substances that barely or do not break down. They are found in a great many products, because they repel both oil and water. Knowledge of the risks is growing. For example, they can affect the immune system, the liver and cholesterol, and can cause kidney and testicular cancer. In the Netherlands there are many thousands of sites that may be contaminated with PFAS. Tackling all of them is impossible because of the scale of the contamination and the high costs. That concerns "hundreds of millions and probably billions", according to Hans Slenders of the PFAS Expertise Centre and Arcadis, which among other things is supervising the remediation of Soesterberg air base. For that reason the twelve provinces and 29 large municipalities have, since 2020 and on the ministry's instructions, been working to identify which sites need remediating as soon as possible. The criterion for such a 'PFAS priority location' is that there must be 'unacceptable risks' to people or the environment. The list is to be finished by 2030. Obvious and well-known locations are also still missing, such as Schiphol, says PFAS expert Chiel Jonker of the University of <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity>. "That is one of the largest PFAS locations in the Netherlands, where contaminated water is being pumped out." According to a spokesperson for the provincie Noord-Holland, there are no "acute risks to people or a threat to drinking water abstraction" here. Jonker disagrees. "Fields and vegetable gardens are irrigated with the water, people swim and fish in it, and it flows into the Amsterdam forest. And why are other airfields on the list but not Schiphol?" Too little knowledge Jonker has also noticed that where PFAS have been found, the list often mentions only PFOS, a highly harmful form of PFAS. "PFOS is never alone. It is always a mixture. You can only make a proper risk analysis if you have the concentrations of the various PFAS substances." For Jonker the matter is clear. "You should not leave this to local authorities. That is not sound. You really need to have the expertise." And that expertise is often lacking in provinces and municipalities. Both Jonker and Slenders call for central direction from <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> to map the risks more clearly. "The PFAS problem is far too complicated to solve locally," says Slenders. "The ministry must take the lead." Major consequences That this is not happening now could have major consequences, Jonker outlines: "There is a danger that on the one hand high-risk locations will be missed, and on the other that other locations will be remediated unnecessarily at great expense." Central direction would also speed up the pace. "Local authorities would then get more tools and a stick behind the door. Under decentralisation nothing is moving forward," says Slenders. According to the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-infrastructuur-en-waterstaat">Infrastructuur en Waterstaat</entity>, municipalities and provinces are aware of the definition of a PFAS priority location and are well able to assess the risks. Which locations are on the priority list? Of the 57 locations, most are already known: (former) airfields, defence sites and fire service training grounds. New locations include, among others, the Rotterdam port area, although it is not yet clear there whether there are unacceptable risks. At the former Valkenburg air base there is similarly no clarity, even though the PFAS contamination was known as early as 2014. It is 'not yet possible to say' whether there are risks to nearby drinking water supplies. Chip manufacturer NXP in Nijmegen discovered PFAS contamination itself, possibly through company fire brigade activities. The municipality expects further investigation by NXP, which itself is not answering questions. Akzo Nobel has remediated the coatings factory in Sassenheim because of historical fires, fire-fighting foam discharges, fire-fighting exercises and spread through the air. There are currently no risks to nearby allotment gardens, but 'investigations are still ongoing'. The locations with the largest contaminated area are in <entity id="org:gemeente-helmond">Helmond</entity>, on the site of the bankrupt Custom Powders (mainly groundwater), and the Oranjekazerne in <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity> (mainly soil).

title: More students want help with money matters, education institutions see
lead: More students are asking their education institution for financial help. That is what more than twenty education institutions tell NOS Stories. For example, vocational colleges (mbo), universities of applied sciences (hbo) and universities see an increase in applications for payment arrangements. They also more often finance certain school supplies and give more advice on money matters. This is in line with a study by the Armoedefonds earlier this year. It showed that nearly 60 percent of poverty relief organisations see an increase in applications from young people. Research by the Nibud also showed that more and more young people say they find it hard to make ends meet. In 2024 this was 40 percent, in 2026 it is 54 percent. A lot of stress "'Money matters' is number one for us," says Sophie Koole, youth worker at mbo Aventus in Apeldoorn. She is referring to the list of conversation topics she covers with students. For example, Koole helped student Fulla Hamash (19) with her money problems. Hamash: "I had a lot of stress from the debts I had. Sophie gave me tips on saving and making overviews, and now things really are getting better." Youth worker Koole hears from young people that they have to work incredibly hard to get by. "Because life is getting more and more expensive for young people." At the same time, young people also more often lose track of their finances. "It is easy to spend money these days. You can do everything with 'pay later'. There is no grip on it anymore. That is a major concern." "We are quite shocked by the increase in requests for help," also says Lotte Meerhoff of the Armoedefonds. "That more young people are seeking help is good, but it also shows once again how many young people struggle with financial problems. And that can really determine your future, in a negative sense." Three part-time jobs NOS Stories spoke with young people who say that, alongside their studies, they have three part-time jobs to get by. There are also examples of young people who want to continue studying, for example by doing a university master's, but who are financially unable to do so. According to the Armoedefonds, nearly a third of poverty relief organisations see that young people cannot start or complete their education because of money problems. Education institutions try to help in all kinds of ways. For example, with payment arrangements, so students do not have to transfer money all at once. Or special funds that finance books or a laptop, for instance. Some courses offer workshops or theatre performances about money. And there are many schools with special money coaches or youth workers. 'More needed' The Armoedefonds welcomes the help, but at the same time the foundation stresses that more is needed. And especially preventive measures, from politics. "Politics needs to come up with a broader approach to prevent young people from falling into poverty," says spokesperson Meerhoff. "We have seen for years that money problems among young people are growing. Then limiting the options for pay later, which politicians are now working on, is not enough. Young people need to have more to spend, so that means raising the minimum wage and student finance." According to Meerhoff, that is especially important for the group of young people who receive no financial support from their parents. They, especially from the age of 18, when you have to handle more money matters yourself, more often struggle with serious money problems. Although a growing group of students is asking for help, talking about money remains a taboo for many young people, research by Humanitas shows, as do many conversations that NOS Stories had with students. Abir and Sam, both 18 and studying at mboRijnland in Leiden, struggle with it. "Say you don't have much to spend and you tell people, they might laugh at you. You kind of feel ashamed of it," says Abir. When Sam's friends do something fun, she sometimes says she has no time. "When actually I just don't have the money. Then they think I'm poor. I want to prevent that." Youth worker Koole sees 'money stress' growing among young people, partly because they do not talk about the subject. "If you think you have to do it all alone, it keeps going round in your head. It is there, but you push it away. And then it can get worse. Then you may get sleepless nights, and as a result you cannot function normally."

title: Cabinet wants to do things differently, such as choosing more often for a 'bloc of parties'
lead: Trust between D66, VVD and CDA has been restored, but at the same time much still needs to be done to make the minority coalition work. That was the message from <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> and the two deputy prime ministers after days of crisis talks. In particular, relations with <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> must change. "Structural agreements must be made on support for the budgets and the tax plan", Jetten said at a press conference. Vice-president of the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity> <entity id="person:sybrand-van-haersma-buma">Sybrand Buma</entity> will help work out how the House and the cabinet can make such agreements. The prime minister spoke of a "Scandinavian model" and said that from now on a clear choice must be made to negotiate with "a bloc of parties" on the left or right. A group of MPs who are considering the way the House of Representatives works recently visited Scandinavian countries to see how a minority cabinet can function. One option is, for example, making informal long-term agreements on a number of major issues. Buma has one month for his work. Less Hague fuss The prime minister further said he hopes for a different dynamic. "Less Hague fuss and internal discussion, more calm and clarity." Jetten also said he takes it to heart that things did not go well: Yesilgöz, VVD deputy prime minister, has "trust and hope" in the process that the coalition will follow. She acknowledges that things have not gone well. "If the financial foundation under the plans has no majority, the substantive matters also get out of balance. That is what has happened", she said. SME package On substance, the three parties have also agreed on something, to meet the VVD halfway. A package of measures will come to support SME entrepreneurs in "investing, innovating and becoming more sustainable", Jetten said. The plans are still being worked out. The minority coalition and the cabinet ran into serious trouble last week, after D66 and CDA reached an agreement with Pro and Volt on an amendment to the tax plan, as a result of which wealthier people will pay somewhat more tax. The VVD said it felt ambushed by this and called the deal "substantively really bad for the Netherlands". The amendment nevertheless won a majority in the House of Representatives, after which the VVD decided to vote against the entire tax plan. No JA21 In the end, D66 and CDA nevertheless managed to secure a majority in that vote too, by concluding an agreement with the opposition parties Denk, 50Plus, the ChristenUnie and Partij voor de Dieren. After a first crisis meeting on Friday, VVD leader Yesilgöz called the minority cabinet "a failed experiment that cannot go on like this". She demanded a "political correction" to the course, which she considered too left-wing. She raised the possibility of adding an extra, right-wing coalition partner, possibly JA21. That was not chosen in the days of crisis talks that followed. Look back here at how the main players reflect on the crisis talks:

title: Cabinet crisis averted with an empty story, coalition carries on for now on willpower alone
lead: After their near-fatal quarrel, D66, VVD and CDA are nonetheless carrying on together on willpower, and on hope of a blessing. Because in substance the four days of crisis talks have produced little. The minority coalition's hope now rests on vice-chair of the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity> <entity id="person:sybrand-van-haersma-buma">Sybrand Buma</entity>, who is to give cooperation with the opposition a nudge. Trust has been restored. That was last night's brief message with which the days-long talks between the coalition parties were concluded. Today an explanation was to come at a press conference from <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> (D66), deputy prime minister Yesilgöz (VVD) and deputy prime minister Van den Brink (CDA). But why they should now trust each other again did not really become clear. A few days ago the main players were still standing face to face. Telling was that Yesilgöz called the minority cabinet on Friday, in fierce tones, a "failed experiment" that "cannot go on like this", just after Jetten had spoken conciliatory words. Tackling the problem Yesilgöz also demanded a "political correction" to the course. A very small correction is now coming; the VVD gets at most 100 million euros more for entrepreneurs. But the biggest hurdle has not been cleared with that, because how exactly are <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> and the coalition to cooperate fruitfully with the opposition? To tackle that problem Buma has been taken on board. The vice-chair of the Raad van State has a month to pull the chestnuts out of the fire. The expectation is mainly that he will look at how you can still make good agreements without opposition parties linking all kinds of topics together. That, the idea goes, has made everything unnecessarily complex in recent times. Jetten said today he hopes relations with <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> will change. "There really needs to be a different dynamic, with less Hague fuss." Ultimately that should lead to "structural agreements" on finances and process. Less bickering, then. Yet another delay The premier blames himself for his cabinet having insisted for too long that broad majorities of a hundred seats could certainly be found. Until now Jetten has been "too nice" and "too optimistic", he himself thinks. From now on it must more often be chosen to negotiate with "a bloc of parties" on the left or right. But which bloc he prefers, Jetten did not say. And that is precisely what opposition parties have been asking for in vain for months. Today too there is complaint that still nothing is being chosen. "The cabinet itself must make that difficult choice", responded Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity>. "This is just more delay", he said about the appointment of Buma. Buma and Heinen in the debate In the House there are doubts about Buma's arrival; is this task not too political for the supposedly neutral head of the Raad van State? In the debate on this crisis, held today, it will be a topic. Incidentally, the position of <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> (VVD, <entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity>) will also be put on the table. The question is whether he lobbied the opposition party Denk last week against his own tax plan. Denk says yes, the VVD denies it. The minister did text Denk, but only to thwart the plan of Pro, the VVD states. Several parties hope for clarification in the debate. Recently 'over right' has proved complicated for the cabinet, mainly because of the linking of topics by JA21, BBB and SGP. 'Over left' also proved impossible because the VVD has been firmly saying no to it since the campaign. Incidentally, a somewhat different tone was struck here today. "Then it really doesn't matter to me whether it is with right or left", said the VVD leader about making agreements on certain topics. But whether anything can be read from this for the future is not clear. It is a tightrope for party leader Yesilgöz. Officials in her party have for some time felt that Pro, for example, should not be categorically excluded, because it can be worked with well enough. Meanwhile the right wing of the VVD is appalled. That side of the party will also not necessarily be able to appreciate today's relaunch, without the VVD having gained much in substance in return. These VVD members mainly feel that the party has had to give up a lot in this coalition, with one of the low points being the tax plan pulled to the left. Near-breach About that tax plan the coalition and cabinet ran into serious trouble last week, after D66 and CDA reached an agreement with Pro and Volt on an amendment, as a result of which wealthy people will pay somewhat more tax. The VVD was not pleased and called the deal "substantively really bad for the Netherlands". The amendment nevertheless received a majority, after which the VVD decided to vote against the entire tax plan. This proved the starting point for four days of crisis talks. Those talks nearly ended in a breach. On Saturday morning it was "really almost over" for the cabinet, it is heard. The fact that practically all of Dutch administration did not want the cabinet to fall is said to have kept the three from it, among other things. 'It is not sellable to send the country back to the polls again', is the basis on which they carry on. A shaky basis and an empty story, then, but the tangle has at least been untangled for now. Perhaps Buma will manage to tie it all together again. He must be finished by mid-December; until then the cabinet can at least carry on.

title: Opposition critical of Buma's role: choice between left and right postponed again
lead: The appointment of <entity id="person:sybrand-van-haersma-buma">Sybrand Buma</entity>, vice-president of the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity>, has been received with little enthusiasm by many opposition parties. This became clear on Tuesday evening during a debate lasting over eight hours on the 'political situation that has arisen', which continued into the night. Pro, SP, PVV, Partij voor de Dieren, BBB and ChristenUnie, among others, have questions about Buma's appointment. Pro and the Partij voor de Dieren believe that <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is once again pushing back the choice for cooperation with opposition parties. "We are back to square one", concluded <entity id="person:christine-teunissen">partijleider Teunissen</entity> of the Partij voor de Dieren. "The only thing that has happened is that a cabinet collapse has been averted", said Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity>. There is relief, however, that no new elections are coming for now. <entity id="person:rob-jetten">Premier Jetten</entity> is convinced that by calling on Buma's help, the minority cabinet will function better. Buma must "sketch possible forms" in which the minority cabinet can cooperate better around "financial decision-making moments". Buma could also provide a framework for future minority cabinets, so the thinking goes. Jetten received many questions during the debate about the request for help. What exactly is he going to do? Isn't the difficult work being outsourced, and shouldn't Prime Minister Jetten do it himself? There is also fear that Buma will end up in a political role when financial choices are made. "Isn't he being used as a pawn?" Volt-<entity id="person:laurens-antonius-josephus-maria-dassen">leider Dassen</entity>, for example, wants to know. No convincing answer Those were questions that the parliamentary leaders Paternotte (D66), Brekelmans (VVD) and Bontenbal (CDA) did not necessarily have a convincing answer to in the debate. Paternotte said it is not the intention for Buma to rewrite the coalition agreement. Brekelmans expressed hope for a "solid financial foundation" and for long-term agreements on defence, for example, but does not know whether it will succeed. "We cannot expect Mr Buma to sort this out just like that. Because it is extremely complicated." See here how some opposition parties view the choice for Buma: Once again, the central question in the debate was: will this minority cabinet choose left or right? With Buma's appointment, that choice is once again being put off indefinitely. Pro leader Klaver hopes the Jetten cabinet will think it over carefully. "You don't need Buma to make choices," said Klaver. "We could start negotiating tomorrow." But Jetten does not intend to say in the short term with which opposition parties they will start negotiations on the next major financial issue, the Spring Memorandum. "No, we are not going to run around like a headless chicken," is Prime Minister Jetten's answer. "We have done that over the past weeks and months." He does promise, however, that the cabinet will make those choices after the Buma report. The messages between VVD and Denk The debate also touched on another sensitive issue: the messages, phone calls and conversations between coalition party VVD and opposition party Denk. It is clear that several VVD members had contact with Denk's MPs on the day of the votes on the tax plan. PVV, Pro, Volt and other opposition parties wanted above all to know whether the VVD tried to have its own tax plan defeated in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The VVD strongly denies this; according to the party, there was only contact about motions and amendments. Opposition parties PVV and Pro called on <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> (<entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity>) to explain his contact with Denk in the House. The minister did not heed this. According to Prime Minister Jetten, this was not necessary either, because he was speaking on behalf of the entire cabinet. A request to make public the communication between Heinen and Denk MPs was also not granted. According to Heinen, these are "confidential political contacts" that are "necessary for the proper functioning of the parliamentary process". 'Clear-cut letter' In the coming weeks it should become clear how the minority cabinet will proceed. Jetten will first write a "clear-cut" letter to Buma about his new assignment. In it, he also says he will take on board the concerns and criticism of the opposition parties. Buma then gets a month to give the minority cabinet a push forward. It is still unknown how Buma will go about his assignment. So it is also not yet clear with whom and where he will hold his talks.

title: Forum voor Democratie uses extreme-right terms most often in House of Representatives
lead: The word 'remigratie' is being uttered more and more often in parliament. This is shown by figures that Nieuwsuur requested from the House of Representatives. Over the past ten years the word came up 115 times, 96 of them since 2024: 53 times Members of Forum voor Democratie (FVD) said it, and 19 times they were PVV members. The word 'omvolking' has also been used most often by FVD members. According to the security services <entity id="org:directoraat-generaal-algemene-inlichtingen-en-veiligheidsdienst">AIVD</entity> and NCTV, right-wing extremist groups use this kind of euphemistic language to influence Dutch society, so that they sound more acceptable. The groups want to undermine the democratic legal order and establish a "white ethnostate", the services say. The services do not name any political parties in their report, but according to experts Forum voor Democratie contributes to the 'normalisation' of extreme-right ideas through its use of language. "Forum is an extreme-right party that poses a threat to the democratic legal order", says historian Robin te Slaa, who recently published a book about FVD titled Flirten met fascisme. "With all its contacts, the party really moves within an extreme-right milieu, both European and national", says Sarah de Lange, professor of Dutch politics at Leiden University. Behind the word 'remigratie' lies a dark world, the experts and the security services contend. "When extreme-right activists and movements refer to remigration, what they actually mean is the deportation of people living in the Netherlands who have a migrant background", says De Lange. According to Te Slaa, the right-wing extremists are aiming for "ethnic cleansing". "To once again ensure a white Europe." 'Legitimate positions' Ralf Dekker, acting parliamentary leader of Forum voor Democratie, says he finds the services' statements "a bit criminalising". "Remigration and omvolking are normal words, and we have legitimate political positions on them", says Dekker. "Omvolking is a factual description; the people of today have a different composition than forty or fifty years ago. You can argue about the extent to which it was deliberate policy to bring that about." According to historian Te Slaa, 'omvolking' expresses an extreme-right, antisemitic conspiracy theory. "The elite, or in some cases explicitly the Jewish elite, is according to the theory deliberately working to replace the originally white population with non-Europeans and people of colour." Forum voor Democratie is currently the only party still using the word 'omvolking' in the House. The PVV stopped doing so in 2024, after it joined the <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity>-Schoof. Even now that PVV leader <entity id="person:geert-wilders">Geert Wilders</entity> is back in opposition, he no longer uses the word in debates. According to <entity id="person:roelof-jan-dekker">fractievoorzitter Dekker</entity> of FVD, who is replacing party leader Lidewij de Vos during her maternity leave, skin colour is "at most an indication of how many people have come from outside". Dekker does not distance himself from a statement by FVD party chairman Thierry Baudet, who said in 2024 that "mass remigration" is needed because a stop on immigration alone is insufficient to "preserve a white Europe". Intervention Other parties in the House of Representatives are struggling with the statements of Forum voor Democratie, according to a survey conducted by Nieuwsuur. Parties on the left feel that the Speaker of the House should intervene when FVD uses the words 'remigratie' or 'omvolking'. "The Speaker of the House must prevent extreme-right language from being normalised in our parliament", says Pro leader Jesse Klaver. Coalition parties D66, VVD and CDA believe it is up to the Speaker of the House to weigh the freedom of Members to speak out against the dignity of the debate. "This is not only about which words are used, but mainly about the message being conveyed with them", says CDA leader Henri Bontenbal. Right-wing parties JA21 and BBB have included 'remigratie' in their election manifestos, following FVD and the PVV. They are not retracting it, not even after the warning from the security services. "We think promoting voluntary remigration is fine", says JA21 spokesman Joost Eerdmans. "But deporting people on grounds of origin, religion or race is reprehensible, and we of course reject it." House of Representatives Speaker Thom van Campen does not want to ban words, he tells Nieuwsuur. "I invite all Members of the House to engage in debate with one another. Because that is what matters: what does someone actually mean by a particular term? What idea lies behind it? That debate is more important than me as chair saying: this is allowed or this is not allowed."

title: Cabinet 'back to square one' after averting crisis, design flaw not repaired
lead: 'Aan de slag' (Get to work) was the title of the coalition agreement with which the minority cabinet of <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> began. That it would be hard work, the ministers had certainly anticipated. Litres of coffee would be needed to win over the opposition. But they went for it. Less than nine months after the cabinet took office, VVD leader Yesilgöz already called the experiment "failed". The cabinet, which wanted to help the Netherlands move forward again, landed after a chaotic period in a deep crisis, which was averted by the skin of its teeth yesterday. The trigger was the tax plan for the coming year, which normally passes without major problems. Or rather, mainly the squabbling between the three coalition parties; the relations between them were never good. Design flaw Even before this coalition began, the design flaw already surfaced, which was also much discussed in yesterday's debate on the crisis. The formation, which lasted about four months, was difficult. First D66 and CDA found each other, then the VVD joined. Immediately there was that division, which nearly cost the cabinet its life. Because who had to be brought in to form a majority cabinet? Was it the largest opposition party Pro (then still GroenLinks-PvdA)? Did JA21 have to join?
